en: Preface to the Supplementary Commentary and Verification of the Meanings of the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules*:

The Traces of the Awakened Sovereign exhaustively employ the understanding of all things to bestow benevolence; the radiant wheel of the Sun of Wisdom follows the depths of sentient emotions to bring them clarity and illumination.

To those who cling to nihilism, one speaks of existence; to those who are sealed by eternalism, one discusses emptiness. One opens the way for the myriad phenomena to coalesce into the ultimate truth, and by departing from the two extremes, the Middle Way is fully revealed.
Thus, the Three Vehicles are universally expounded, the Two Truths are equally encompassed, and principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated.
Speech and silence constitute transformation. When the rainbow light subsided, the eyes of the human and celestial ones were lost.

As the oral teachings were transmitted, the bodies and minds of both ordinary beings and sages remained dependent on conditions. Times shifted and eras changed, yet the natures and characteristics remained distinct; Mañjuśrī and Maitreya differed in their lineages.
Nāgārjuna and Vasubandhu assisted his governance. One should not say that the river was divided for drinking water; rather, one should reflect on how the roaring rock was turned to mud.

Although the clouds and the moon are fundamentally the same, they cannot avoid being distinct according to the valleys and mountains. Thus, Vasubandhu’s school of thought condensed the hundred fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* into the *Uddāna*.
Dharmapāla, pitying the deluded, composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* as an exposition of the thirty verses, bringing forth [the true meaning].
The subtle principles are profound and mysterious; [this work] elucidates the esoteric scriptures of the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya).
The ten masters have penetrated them with precision, and the hundred fascicles encompass them thoroughly. They are categorized and classified, each following its own source.

Master Xuanzang has blended these ten commentaries and translated them into ten fascicles, thereby making it so that although the texts differ, their meanings are unified, as if composed by a single master. Although they are now concise and refined, they remain difficult to memorize. To create...

The *Verses on the Eight Consciousnesses* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī) unifies its threads, while this work divides it into four chapters to encompass its principles. Although there were previously existing commentaries, the transcribed versions contained many errors.
Dharma Master Tai of Lushan collated and supplemented them to form a complete edition, which was subsequently carved for publication.

This humble writer has long studied this scripture, yet has certainly not reached its ultimate depths; however, he knows that this commentary frequently cites passages from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and as for those cited...
There are points regarding the meaning that have not yet been exhausted; these are here further extracted. The sequence of the exegesis is likewise supplemented by citations from the treatise itself.
Therefore, this is titled *The Supplementary Notes on the Proof of the Meaning of the Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules*.
It was composed by the śramaṇa Mingyu of Fuci from Western Sichuan on the Dragon Boat Festival day of the Jiyou year of the Wanli era at the left side of the Mumo Pavilion in Moling.
*The Supplementary Commentary on the Proof of the Meaning of the Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules*,
composed by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty;
with verses elucidated and supplemented by the Dharma Master Puthai of Lushan.
Verified by the Chan Monk Mingyu of Western Shu. Regarding the meaning:

these eight consciousnesses have fixed numbers for their modes of activity (*ākāra*), mental factors (*caitta*), objects of perception (*ālambana*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), magnitude (*pramāṇa*), realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and all phenomena (*dharma*);

therefore, they are called "rules" (*niyama*). The eight consciousnesses are: first, the eye-consciousness; second, the ear-consciousness; third, the nose-consciousness; fourth, the tongue-consciousness... [and so forth].
Consciousness: (1) the five body-consciousnesses, (2) the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), (3) the *manas* consciousness, and (4) the *ālaya* consciousness.
The first six derive their names from their bases; the seventh receives its designation based on its association; and the eighth is named according to its functional capacity.

Regarding those that derive their names from their bases: "base" (*āśraya*) has the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*). This means that the first six consciousnesses are established by name based upon their faculties, because they possess five meanings. First:
It is based on its object; it is called "eye-consciousness" because it is consciousness that relies upon the eye.

Furthermore, consciousness arises by depending on the locus of the eye, and because consciousness exists only when the eye exists. Why is this so? Because when the eye-faculty exists, eye-consciousness necessarily arises.
It is not because one is not blind that visual consciousness necessarily arises even in the dark; for those who are blind cannot see.
Second, regarding the meaning of "arising": it is called "eye-consciousness" because it is the consciousness produced by the eye.
It is due to the transformation of the eye that the consciousness also transforms, for although the form (color) does not transform, the consciousness undergoes transformation. Kātyāyanīputra says:
First, the disease of the Malla people impairs the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*); because of this impairment, one perceives colors such as yellow when looking at blue and so forth.

Second, it has the sense of "belonging to": the consciousness that belongs to the eye is therefore called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*), since it arises by following the faculty through the seeds of consciousness.

It is not merely the seeds of form that follow; the seeds of consciousness likewise follow along. Fourth, it has the sense of "assisting": it is named so because it assists the consciousness of the eye.

Visual consciousness [functions] with respect to that visual faculty because it brings about its benefit or harm. Why is this so? It is because the faculty, conjoined with consciousness, undergoes experience that causes the faculty to be benefited or harmed;
it is not the case that the objective field does so. Fifth, "according to the meaning," as in the case of the consciousness of the eye.
Therefore, it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*), because it is comprised within the category of sentient beings, whereas those [objects of] form are certainly insentient.
Because the sense organs (*indriya*) possess five superior qualities, they are designated as the "basis" (*āśraya*). Just as it is with eye-consciousness, so it is with the other consciousnesses.
Regarding the establishment of names based on association: the seventh consciousness is called *manas* because it is associated with the four afflictions. In its full form, it should be...

*Kliṣṭamanas* is translated here as "defiled mind. This refers to that which is always accompanied by the four afflictions—namely, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), [self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-tṛṣṇā*)]—and is therefore called "defiled. Because it constantly and thoroughly deliberates, it is termed "mind" (*manas*).

Furthermore, because it is capable of discerning objects, it is also termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). Question: How does this differ from the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)? Answer: This [defiled mind] maintains...

The *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) explanation: as with the name "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*), consciousness is itself the mind (*manas*). This means that this seventh [consciousness] is a *karmadhāraya*, because its essential nature directly maintains the activity of constant and thorough deliberation (*manana*).

As for "like the storehouse consciousness," the essence of the eighth consciousness directly maintains the meaning of containing and storing the three [natures]. It is also called a *svabhāvadhāraṇakarmadhāraya* (appositional compound maintaining the essence) and a *karmadhāraṇakarmadhāraya* (appositional compound maintaining the activity).

Therefore, the essence of this consciousness is itself the mind. The *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) explanation: as with "eye-consciousness" and so forth, consciousness is distinct from the mind. This means that the sixth [consciousness] is called a *tatpuruṣa*; the mind-faculty (*manas*) is the primary factor, serving as the basis for the mental consciousness.

Just as the eye is the primary factor and the basis for visual consciousness, both are designated as "basis" and "that which depends on the basis," forming a *tatpuruṣa* compound (possessive determinative). Therefore, the essence of that consciousness is distinct from the *manas*.

Nevertheless, because various sacred teachings fear this might be confused with other [meanings], they designate the seventh [consciousness] solely by the name *manas*. Furthermore, the name *manas* is employed to distinguish it from *citta* and *vijñāna*:

*citta* refers to accumulation (*saṃcita*), *vijñāna* refers to discernment (*prativijñapti*), while the *manas* is merely deliberation (*manana*). Since it lacks those two meanings, it is called only *manas*. Alternatively, [it may be intended that...]
This is to clarify that because it serves as the immediate support for that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is simply called "mind" (*manas*).
Regarding the designation based on its functional capacity: the eighth consciousness possesses the threefold capacity of a storehouse and is thus named *ālaya*.

Paramārtha, following the literal meaning of the name, translates it as "non-perishing consciousness" (*amūḷha-vijñāna*), taking the sense of "not being lost. Xuanzang, following the meaning, translates it as "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*), taking the sense of "containing and storing."

Regarding the meaning: from the perspective of maintaining seeds (*bīja*), it is called the "capable store" (*ālaya*); from the perspective of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is called the "object stored";
and because the seven [consciousnesses] grasp it as a self, it is called the "appropriated store. It receives the name *ālayavijñāna* due to these three meanings. As for "rules and compasses":

a compass (*gui*) is the instrument for making perfect circles, while a square (*ju*) is the instrument for making perfect squares. The *Zitong* (Compendium of Characters) states: "The cognitive capacity of a man must..."
It accords with the compass and the square. Thus, the compass follows the husband, and the square follows the arrow; "arrow" signifies rectitude.

This refers to these forty-eight verses, which precisely determine that each of the eight consciousnesses possesses distinct differences in its objects, measures, natures, and realms, thereby ensuring they are pure and unmixed.
Therefore, it is so named. The eight consciousnesses are the supported (the basis), while the compass and the square are the supporting (the means). The supported...
Based on this principle, that which is supported is the meaning of "container. Therefore, it is called "the regulations of the eight consciousnesses.

This is an *adhāralopika-tatpuruṣa* (dependent-determinative) compound, wherein both the supporting and the supported are made manifest. The supplementary commentary proving this meaning appears at the end of the preface; it shall not be explained again here.
Regarding the first five consciousnesses, the verse states:
"Their nature is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and they range across the three moral natures.

This verse concerns the first five consciousnesses. Among the three types of objects, they perceive only "nature-objects" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). Among the three types of cognition, they are exclusively direct perception. And as for the three... [text fragment ends]

The nature [of objects] is common to both [the subjective and objective]. As for their spheres (ālambana), there are three: namely, the nature-sphere (svabhāva-viṣaya), the solitary-reflection sphere (pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya), and the substance-possessing sphere (sadravya-viṣaya).

The verse speaks of the "nature-sphere. "Nature" (svabhāva) has the meaning of "reality"; it refers to the actual sense faculties and their objects: earth, water, fire, and wind; and form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Both the subject and object—these eight factors—all possess substantiality, because they are portions of real phenomena. That is to say, this nature-sphere arises from real seeds.

There are entities possessing real function; these are presently existing real dharmas. Among the two types of transformation, because they are transformations due to causes and conditions, they differ from "sole-imaginary" (*kevala-pratibimba*) and "with-substantive-object" (*sadravya-viṣaya*) objects, which arise from the transformation of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Within the five stages of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), these are precisely the "consciousness-only as the object.

There are also three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). The verse mentions "direct perception," meaning that which is currently present.
There are three meanings: first, it refers to the present, thereby excluding the past and future; second, it refers to that which is manifest, thereby excluding seeds;

third, it refers to that which currently exists, thereby excluding phenomena lacking substantiality. "Māna" (measure) means to measure; it is a term defined by its standard application, referring to the mind with respect to its object.

Because it does not err in measuring and determining the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, it is called "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*); here, however, it is said that direct perception does not involve measurement.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "For example, when the light of the eye clearly perceives an object before it, that light is perfectly complete and free from aversion or attachment.

This can be cited as proof for the meaning that direct perception is non-conceptual. This is because, at the time the first five consciousnesses engage their objects, they are devoid of [conceptualization].
Because it is clearly manifest and free from obscuration, one attains the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object; therefore, it is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

If "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) pertains to the object and "perception" (*kṣa*) pertains to the mind, this follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis. Although the mind arises from the object, the object is inferior and the mind is superior.

Because the mind is superior, it only then manifests the name of the object; because perception is superior, one thereby understands the meaning of "direct. Thus, it is said that superiority and inferiority depend [on the mind].

This clarifies the *upapada-śeṣa* (dependent) analysis. It is like a father giving birth to a son; because the son’s name is "victorious," it reveals the father’s name. This is the dependent [analysis].

Alternatively, both [terms] belong to the mind (*citta*), which is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analysis. That is to say, upon the measure of mind (*cittamātra*), it directly maintains and manifests the activity (*karman*);

thus it is called "the essence maintains the activity" (*tattva-karma-dhāraya*). Alternatively, "manifestation" (*pratyakṣa*) belongs to the sense organ (*indriya*) and "measure" (*māna*) belongs to the mind; this is the *tatpuruṣa* (genitive) analysis.

This is an *adhikaraṇasaptamī* (locative determinative) compound. It refers to the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). They receive their name based on their faculties (*indriya*). Since the faculties upon which they rely act as conditions to produce the consciousnesses, they possess the sense of "host" (*adhi-karaṇa*).
The mind-essence (*citta-mātra*) that relies [upon them] arises and ceases, undergoing transformation; thus it possesses the sense of "guest" (*adhy-āśrita*).

Therefore, it is said that because the "reliant" and the "relied upon" are manifested, it is an *adhikaraṇasaptamī* compound. As for what constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is said: non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
If it constitutes the essence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), why is it non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)? It is said:

when the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) correctly cognize an object while remaining free from names and categories, this is called "non-conceptual. Therefore, by means of this wisdom, it constitutes the essence of direct perception.

The *Nyāyamukha* states that there are four kinds of direct perception: first, the five sensory consciousnesses; second, the simultaneous mental consciousness; third, the various... [text fragment ends].

The essence of the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of each mind and mental factor, as well as the four types of concentrated minds—these four are all objects realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and are devoid of conceptual construction;
thus, they are termed "direct perception. Therefore, among the three types of valid cognition, the first five consciousnesses are exclusively direct perception.

The verse mentions the "three natures," namely: the virtuous nature (*kuśalatva*), the non-virtuous nature (*akuśalatva*), and the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛtatva*). These refer to the aforementioned first five consciousnesses.
The three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—are all equally applicable. Why is this? Because the nature of the five consciousnesses is not constant or uniform;

when they encounter a wholesome object, their nature is wholesome; when encountering an unwholesome object, the consciousness is likewise unwholesome; and during moments of indetermination, it is indeterminate.
Consciousness itself is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, the first five consciousnesses are all compatible with the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

Regarding the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) where the first five consciousnesses reside, as stated in the verse: "The three—eye, ear, and body—reside in two stages. These three—the eye, ear, and body—exist in the nine stages of the three realms (*tri-dhātu*), specifically residing only in two [stages].

The realms (dhātu) reside within two stages: namely, the Stage of Mixed Dwelling of the Five Destinies in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu), and the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Seclusion in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
It is called the "Desire Realm" because it possesses food, drink, sleep, and sexual desire. [The five destinies therein are] the celestial destiny, the human destiny, and the animal destiny.
The hungry ghosts (preta) and those in the hells dwell together in the same place; therefore, they are called "mixed dwellings.

Although the various devas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) still possess unextinguished mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta), because their intention lies in extinguishing these through tainted meditative concentration (sāsrava-dhyāna) and they exist as mere physical forms, it is called the "form realm."

One attains the first dhyāna. Although one has not yet entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one has already become free from the various sufferings of birth associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has attained the joy of the tranquil stages of the higher realms;
therefore, it is called "joy and bliss born of seclusion" (*vivekaja-prītisukha*). Why do the three higher dhyānas lack the eye-faculty and the others?

It is said: Because the three consciousnesses do not arise in the aforementioned third dhyāna due to the absence of vitarka and vicāra, it is maintained that in the first dhyāna, when one has not yet entered meditative absorption, there is vitarka and vicāra;
thus, the three consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, exist. When one has already entered absorption, there is no vitarka and only vicāra remains;
lacking one of these two, [the consciousnesses] do not arise. In the second dhyāna and above, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra; as both are absent, they do not arise. Question: The five...
Consciousness does not associate with vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). Why is it that when there is no vitarka and vicāra, the three consciousnesses do not arise? It is said:

although vitarka and vicāra do not associate with the five [sensory] consciousnesses, they do associate with the sixth mental consciousness. Furthermore, the sixth consciousness serves as the condition for the preceding five;
this is called the "basis of discrimination. When the mind discriminates, there must necessarily be vitarka and vicāra. If there were no vitarka and vicāra, the mind...
There is no discrimination. If there is no discrimination, the first five [consciousnesses] do not arise, because consciousness does not arise when even one condition is lacking.

In this verse, the realms and stages of the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses are omitted by way of abbreviation; they exist only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), specifically in the stage where the five destinies dwell together.
Why are the nose and tongue absent in the higher realms? Answer: Because the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue [depend upon] odors, tastes, and tangibles...

The three objects—odor, taste, and touch—are the substance of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). Since edible food is loathed by those in the dhyāna heavens, the objects of odor, taste, and touch are entirely absent in the higher realms;
consequently, consciousness does not arise there either.

The universal, the specific, the eleven wholesome, the two intermediate, the eight great, and greed, hatred, and delusion—these are the mental factors associated with the five sensory consciousnesses as stated in the first five verses of the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "They always arise based on the mind (*citta*), are associated with the mind, and are bound to the mind;
therefore they are called 'mental concomitants' (*caitta*). Just as things belonging to a self are designated as 'mine,' so too... [the mind... regarding the mind...

Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*), the mind (*citta*) grasps only its general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). As for the mental factors (*caitasika*), they also grasp its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and assist in accomplishing the mind's activity;
thus, they receive the name "mental factors. Although all mental factors are identical in their name and meaning, there are six categories (*ṣatsthāna*) of distinct types.
That is to say, there are five universal [mental factors], five object-specific ones, eleven wholesome ones, six afflictions, twenty secondary afflictions, and four indeterminate ones;
together they total fifty-one. What is meant by "universal"? It is said: "Universal" means all-pervasive, and "factors" (saṃskāra) refers to mental concomitants;
thus they are called "universal factors. This is because they are found present together in all states of mind. What...
They are called "distinctive objects" (*viṣaya-viniyata*) because they arise by taking distinct and specific objects as their conditions. What is meant by "wholesome states" (*kuśala-bhūmi*)?

It is so called because they can only arise within a wholesome mind. What is meant by "afflictions" (*kleśa*)? It is so called because their nature is subsumed under the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*).

What are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)? It is said: they are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the primary afflictions, as they are subsumed under specific states. What is meant by "indeterminate" (*aniyata*)? It is said:
because they are indeterminate with respect to both the wholesome and the defiled. Among these, the first five consciousnesses lack only the indeterminate category within the six states.
Among the fifty-one [mental factors], only thirty-four [are included]; the remaining seventeen are excluded because they are mutually contradictory.
Among the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*), the first is attention (*manaskāra*). Its nature is that which can arouse the mind, and its function is to direct the mind toward an object.
This single dharma has two functions: when the mind has not yet arisen, it arouses the mind so that it arises; once the mind has already arisen, [it directs it].
It is called *manasikāra* (attention) because it draws [the mind] toward its object. Why does it draw only the mind? It is said:
although it can also give rise to mental factors (*caitta*), because the mind is the primary [subject], it is described only as drawing the mind. Second, *sparśa* (contact):

it has the nature of causing the mind and mental factors to contact their objects, and its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "volition and so forth," the *Pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* states that it refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
There are seventy-three factors, all of which have contact (*sparśa*) as their basis; therefore, [the text] mentions volition (*cetanā*) and so forth.

Volition is predominant within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and thus it is cited here to include the others. Third, sensation (*vedanā*): its nature is the experience of objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral;
its function is to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), because it gives rise to the desires for union, separation, or neither. Fourth, perception (*saṃjñā*): it is that which can...
Regarding its object, it has the nature of grasping images and the function of establishing various names and conventions;
for only by establishing the specific characteristics of an object can one subsequently give rise to various names and conventions.

Fifth is volition (*cetanā*), which has the nature of causing the mind to engage in activity and the function of directing the mind toward wholesome factors and so forth; for it is able to take up the correct causes and other characteristics of an object and impel [the mind].

They direct the mind to perform virtuous deeds and so forth. These five aforementioned factors are called "universal" (*sarvatraga*) because the mind can function throughout the four "all-encompassing" categories:

namely, all natures (i.e., the three natures such as wholesome and so forth), all stages (i.e., all stages of ordinary beings and sages), all times (i.e., long and short durations), and all [consciousnesses] together (i.e., the eight consciousnesses).
Because these are universal, they are designated as "universal" factors. As for the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*):
Among these, the first is *chanda* (desire). Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the longing for an object of pleasure; its function (*karman*) is to serve as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*).

Furthermore, there are three meanings of "object of pleasure": First, according to one interpretation, "object of pleasure" refers to an object that is desirable (*abhirati-viṣaya*), because desire does not arise toward objects that are loathsome.

Second, according to another interpretation, "object of pleasure" refers to an object that is sought after (*paryeṣita-viṣaya*), because one seeks union with or separation from objects that are either desirable or loathsome. Regarding this...

Regarding the object of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*): it is consistently free from desire. There is a sense in which it is "pleasing" (*abhipreta*), meaning that one wishes to contemplate it; however, if one does not wish to contemplate it, there is no desire at all.
Based on these three points, desire (*chanda*) is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). Second, resolve (*adhimokṣa*) [functions] with respect to a determined object.

Its nature is the act of holding [an object] in mind. Its function is to be unshakable by others. Therefore, it is entirely absent in relation to objects of doubt and is not a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*).
As for the three types of mindfulness (*smṛti*): its nature is to cause the mind to clearly remember and not forget an object previously experienced.

Its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That is to say, by repeatedly recollecting and maintaining objects previously perceived, it prevents them from being lost and thereby induces concentration.

Regarding objects that have never before been experienced, mindfulness does not arise at all; even regarding those previously experienced, it cannot be clearly remembered, and thus mindfulness does not arise.

Therefore, it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). As for concentration (*samādhi*), its nature is to cause the mind to focus one-pointedly on the object of observation without distraction, and its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom (*jñāna*).
That is to say, regarding objects that are observed as being either beneficial, detrimental, or neither, it causes the mind—
Focused and undistracted, based upon this, there arises the wisdom of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-jñāna*). If one is not focused, concentration (*samādhi*) does not arise;
therefore, it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). Fifth, wisdom (*prajñā*) has the nature of discriminating the object under investigation and the function of severing doubt.
Because it lacks discrimination within a mind that is ignorant regarding objects not under investigation, it is not included among the universal factors. (The ten wholesome [mental factors]...)
First, the *Triṃśikā* states: "The wholesome consists of faith, shame, and dread; the three roots such as non-attachment; diligence, pliancy, and heedfulness; equanimity, and non-harming.
Regarding the first, faith (*śraddhā*): it is a deep conviction, aspiration, and desire toward what is real, virtuous, and capable;
its intrinsic nature is the clarity of the mind; its function is to counteract lack of faith and to delight in the wholesome. Briefly stated, there are three types of faith.
First is faith in actual existence, which means having deep faith and acceptance regarding the reality and principles of all phenomena.
Second is faith in virtuous qualities, which means having deep faith and aspiration regarding the true and pure virtues of the Three Jewels.
Third is faith in capability, which means having deep faith that all mundane and supramundane virtues possess the power to be attained and accomplished, thereby giving rise to hope. By means of...

This counters the lack of faith in the Abhidharma and leads to a delight in realizing and practicing mundane and supramundane virtues. Question: "Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which is the cause of faith;
"delightful desire" (*chanda*) refers to aspiration, which is the fruit of faith. What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this faith that establishes them? Answer:
Is it not already stated that its nature is the purity of mind (*citta-viśuddhi*)? This nature is clear and limpid, and it is capable of purifying the mind and other mental factors.
Because the mind is supreme, it is designated by the name "purity of mind. It is like the water-clearing jewel, which is able to purify turbid water. Regarding the two types of *hrī* (shame):

based on the power of one's own self and the Dharma, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the honoring and revering of the noble and the good. Its function (*karman*) is to counteract the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and to bring to rest unwholesome conduct.
"Self" refers to one's own person; "Dharma" refers to the teachings. [The practitioner] says: "With such a body as mine, understanding such a Dharma, how could I..."
It is that which produces various evils. Regarding the three types of shame (*hrī*): its nature is to disregard and reject violence and evil by relying on worldly power;
it functions as the antidote to lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and has the activity of ceasing unwholesome conduct. "Worldly power" refers to the censure and reproach of the world.

"Disregard and rejection" means disregarding those who possess evil and not associating with them, and rejecting the karma of unwholesome dharmas and not performing them. It is non-greed and so forth.

These are equal to hatred and delusion; these three are called roots because they are preeminent in producing wholesome states. The three unwholesome roots are their direct antidotes. Regarding non-attachment (*alobha*):
its nature is the absence of clinging toward existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence (*bhavopakarana*). Its function is to counteract greedy attachment and to perform wholesome deeds.
"Existence" refers to the three realms of existence as the fruit, and "requisites for existence" refers to the causes; thus, it is non-attachment toward both cause and effect within the three realms.
Therefore: Fifth, non-hatred (*adveṣa*) has the nature of being free from resentment toward suffering and the causes of suffering; its function is to counteract hatred and to perform wholesome deeds.
"Suffering" refers to the fruit of suffering, while "the causes of suffering" refers to its conditions; it consists in not feeling hatred toward either the cause or the fruit of suffering.
Sixth, non-delusion (*amoha*) has the nature of clear understanding regarding all phenomena and principles; its function is to counteract ignorance and to perform wholesome deeds.
Seventh is diligence (*vīrya*). Its nature is valor (*dhṛti*) in the practice of cultivation and abandonment regarding the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome;

it counteracts laziness and has the function of fulfilling the wholesome. "Valor" indicates superior progress, distinguishing it from all defiled phenomena; "firmness" (*dhairya*) indicates purity, distinguishing it from the pure-neutral.

This clarifies that diligence is comprised solely within the category of the wholesome. Eighth is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); it is the removal of heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*), and its function is to bring about adaptability (*karmanyatā*).
Pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) has the nature of being capable and fit for action. Its function is to counteract lethargy (*styāna*) and to effect the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

This means that it suppresses and eliminates those factors that obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*), thereby causing the basis upon which one relies to become transformed into a state of ease. Furthermore, it is said that freedom from heaviness is called "lightness" (*laghu*), and being well-regulated is called "tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*).
It possesses the capacity to endure and the ability to bear; it causes the body and mind, which serve as the basis, to be freed from coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).

Because it brings about peace and security, non-negligence (*apramāda*) consists of the nine forms of heedfulness and the three roots of virtue. Its intrinsic nature is the guarding and cultivation regarding that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be cultivated.
Its function is to counteract negligence and to bring to completion all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds.

That is to say, these four factors—namely, the aforementioned [four wholesome roots]—are able to guard against and cultivate both abandonment and cultivation; thus they are called non-negligence. It does not possess a separate substantial entity.

Because they have distinct characteristics. Equanimity of the ten applications (*daśa-prahāṇasaṃskāra*) has the nature of causing the mind to abide in a state that is even, upright, and effortless through the faculty of vigor and the three [other] faculties.
Its function is to counteract restlessness and to cause the mind to dwell in tranquility. This is called equanimity of application (*prayoga-upekṣā*).

Within the five aggregates, it is included in the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); therefore, it is termed "dwelling in tranquility. Regarding the meaning of making the mind even: by means of equanimity, the mind is freed from dullness (*laya*).
At the time of agitation, the initial mind is equanimous, the subsequent mind is upright, and the final state is effortless.
This single dharma also constitutes four dharmas. That which enables tranquility consists of these four dharmas; that which is made tranquil refers to the meaning of mental equanimity and so forth.
Eleventh is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*): it has the nature of non-aversion and does not inflict injury or affliction upon sentient beings. It is able to counteract...

Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) has the function of counteracting harm; its activity consists in compassion for sentient beings. It is essentially non-hatred (*adveṣa*), which, with respect to sentient beings, refrains from causing injury or affliction, and is thus designated as "non-harming.
Non-hatred is the direct opposite of hatred that takes the form of taking life, whereas non-harming is the direct antithesis of the harm that consists in injuring or afflicting beings.
Non-hatred bestows happiness, while non-harming extracts suffering; this is said to be the distinction between these two in terms of their coarse characteristics. This is the principle.
In reality, there is no hatred (*dveṣa*). It truly possesses its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and does not harm.
It is provisionally established based on a portion of that [nature] in order to manifest the distinct characteristics of compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Because these two are superior in bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings, among the twenty-six types of afflictions—both root and derivative—only thirteen are present within the first five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). That is to say, of the six root afflictions, only the first three are included, because pride (*māna*)...

Doubt and [wrong] view arise only through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because they are not direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*). Among the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), these two belong to the latter ten;

the former ten minor secondary afflictions (*parīttakleśabhūmika*) arise from deliberate conceptualization rather than spontaneously. These twenty secondary afflictions are divided into small, medium, and great categories.
Because they arise simultaneously with their own kind, pervade both natures, and pervade all defiled minds—since they possess all three of these meanings, they are termed "great" (*mahā-kuśala*);

possessing only one, they are termed "middling"; and possessing none, they are termed "small. Regarding the two natures, these refer to the unwholesome nature (*akuśala*) and the obscured nature (*nivṛta*).

The eight factors such as restlessness (*auddhatya*) are termed "great" because they possess all three of the aforementioned meanings. As for lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), [they are also termed great].

They arise simultaneously with their own kind within a single [mental] moment. Because the ten factors such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth arise individually, they lack the quality of arising simultaneously with their own kind.

Being exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), they lack both the qualities of being pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and being defiled by nature (*kliṣṭa*). Since they lack the quality of being "obscured" (*nivṛta*)—as they do not pervade all defiled minds—they lack all three characteristics [of the major secondary afflictions].
Therefore, they are called "minor secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*). They are associated exclusively with the sixth consciousness, the mental faculty (*manovijñāna*). This...

[The Great Grounds] do not explain [the specific meanings]. Among the two [types of secondary afflictions], first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) has the nature of disregarding one’s own dharma and slighting or rejecting the virtuous and good;

its function is to obstruct shame and to cause the growth of unwholesome conduct. Second, lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) has the nature of disregarding the world and honoring or valuing the violent and evil;
its function is to obstruct dread of blame and to cause the growth of unwholesome conduct. [These are the] Great Secondary Afflictions.
Among these eight, first, *auddhatya* (restlessness) has the nature of causing the mind to be non-quiescent with respect to its objects;
its function is to obstruct equanimity (*upekṣā*) and *śamatha*. Second, *styāna* (sloth) has the nature of making the mind incapable of functioning with respect to its objects;
its function is to obstruct pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and *vipaśyanā*. Third, *āśraddhya* (lack of faith) is the lack of conviction regarding reality, virtue, and capability.
Lassitude (*kausīdya*) has the nature of mental impurity; its function is to obstruct pure faith. This is because one who lacks faith is generally prone to indolence.
Fourth, lassitude has the nature of slothfulness regarding the practice of virtue and the abandonment of non-virtue within the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Its function is to obstruct diligence and increase defilement; that is to say, because one who is indolent causes defilements to flourish.

Fifth, heedlessness (*pramāda*) has the nature of being dissolute and incapable of guarding against or cultivating the categories of the defiled and the pure. Its function is to obstruct non-heedlessness and to serve as the basis for increasing evil and diminishing good.
That is to say, due to indolence, as well as greed, hatred, and delusion, one is unable to guard against or cultivate [the path] regarding the defiled.
The dharmas of the pure category are collectively termed *pramāda* (heedlessness); they do not possess a separate substantial entity. Regarding the six types of *muṣitasmṛtitā* (loss of mindfulness):
its nature is the inability to clearly remember various objects of cognition; its function is to obstruct right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and to serve as the basis for distraction.

As for the "covering" (*nīvaraṇa*) of loss of mindfulness, it is because the mind is distracted. One interpretation holds that loss of mindfulness is subsumed under one part of mindfulness itself, being described as associated with afflictions.

Regarding "loss of mindfulness" (*muṣitasmṛti*): one interpretation holds that it is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*), because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that this is a factor of delusion;
since delusion causes the loss of mindfulness, it is termed "loss of mindfulness.

Another interpretation holds that it is subsumed under portions of both [ignorance and distraction], because the two preceding passages provide an abbreviated description by implication, and the treatise further states that this pervades all defiled minds. Furthermore, it has no separate substantial entity. (7) Distraction (*vikṣepa*).
[Distraction] has the nature of causing the mind to wander among various objects of focus;

its function is to obstruct right concentration and to serve as the basis for faulty wisdom (*duṣprajñā*), because one who is distracted gives rise to faulty wisdom. (8) Lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) has the nature of misinterpreting the object under observation;
its function is to obstruct right knowledge and to lead to regret and transgression, because one who lacks clear comprehension frequently commits such regrets and transgressions.
One interpretation states that it is subsumed under a portion of wisdom (*prajñā*); another interpretation states that it is subsumed under a portion of delusion (*moha*);
yet another interpretation states that it is subsumed under portions of both. Therefore, lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) does not exist as a separate substantial entity.

The three—heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), and lack of clear comprehension—are nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*). The other five are substantially existent (*dravyasat*). Regarding greed, hatred, and delusion: these are the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
These are three of the six [afflictions]. First, greed (*lobha*): its nature is attachment to existence and the requisites of existence;
its function is to obstruct non-greed and to produce suffering, because the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) arise through the power of craving. Second, hatred (*dveṣa*):
its nature is the intensification of resentment toward suffering and the requisites of suffering; it functions to obstruct non-hatred and serves as the basis for unpeaceful states and evil conduct.
Its function is to cause the body and mind to suffer from feverish affliction and to give rise to various unwholesome karmas, because its nature is non-virtuous.

○ Third, delusion (*moha*) has the nature of being confused and obscured regarding all principles and phenomena; its function is to obstruct non-obstruction and to serve as the basis for all defilements.
That is to say, through ignorance (*avidyā*), one gives rise to doubt, false views, greed, and other primary and secondary afflictions.
Karma is that which can summon future births because it is a defiled phenomenon. Question: Why do the five consciousnesses lack pride (*māna*) and the other [afflictions]?

Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because pride and the others arise through weighing (*tula-nā*) and so forth. The *Suyao cheng weishi lun* (俗詮) says: "Weighing and so forth refer to deliberation and investigation;
pride and the others include doubt and views. That is to say, pride arises from weighing, doubt arises from deliberation, and views [arise from]..."

Because they arise from discursive investigation, the three [afflictions] beginning with pride are all conceptually arisen (*vikalpita-utpanna*) and do not coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

Why are anger (*krodha*) and the others absent? It is said: the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that the ten minor [afflictions] are coarse and violent, and thus do not exist within the five sensory consciousnesses. Why are the indeterminate [afflictions] absent? It is said:
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) are associated exclusively with the sixth consciousness, for they are not among the five [sensory] dharmas.

Furthermore, it says that vitarka and vicāra take the meanings of "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth as their objects of cognition (*ālambana*), and are not the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*), because the latter do not take the meanings of name-bodies and so forth as their objective domains (*viṣaya*).
The five consciousnesses share a common reliance upon the pure material sense organs (*rūpa-indriya*).

This verse [explains] how the first five consciousnesses arise based on their respective organs and the significance of their names. Regarding the term "pure material" (*viśuddha-rūpa*), it serves to distinguish them from the "dust-like" (*rajas-ābhāsa*) organs.

Furthermore, the phrase "relying on the organ" distinguishes them from relying on the object (*viṣaya*); for the object is merely the focal point (*ālambana*) and lacks the functional capacity to initiate consciousness. As it is said:

When the sense organs (indriya) are impaired, even if an object is present, consciousness does not arise; because it is the organ alone that can produce [consciousness], it is said to be "dependent on the organ.
It is not the "dust" (rajas), for that is false and subject to damage, and thus is called "floating" (fu).
Furthermore, because it lacks the functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is termed "dust. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The eye is like a cluster of grapes; the ear..."
The nose is like a pair of hanging claws; the tongue is like a newly waning crescent moon; and the body and forehead are like a waist-drum. This is what is meant.
As for that which relies on pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*), it is also termed the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

This refers to a portion of pure matter within the eye and other sense organs, which, like pure clarified butter (*sarpis*), possesses this nature such that the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth arise when it is present, and do not arise when it is absent. It illuminates the object and gives rise to consciousness.
Because it fulfills the function of a faculty (*indriya*), it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*). It differs from the ephemeral [senses], which are false and subject to decay;
this [faculty] is not subject to decay, and is thus also called "supreme. It differs from the ephemeral senses, which lack seeing, hearing, and so forth;
this [faculty] is capable of cognition, and is thus also called "supreme. For example, the eye can see forms, the ear can hear sounds, the nose can smell odors, and the tongue can taste flavors.
It is the body that is able to perceive touch. The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states: "The capacity for color within consciousness is reasonably termed the five faculties (*indriya*).
This capacity and the objective form have been mutual causes since beginningless time. The treatise itself explains: "Because it can produce consciousness, one infers the existence of the faculty;
this is merely a capacity and is not something externally constructed. It further states: "This capacity of the faculty..."
Yes. The objective forms of the external realm and their functional capacities have served as reciprocal causes since beginningless time.

That is to say, when these functional capacities reach their stage of maturation, they give rise to the five internal objective forms upon the manifesting consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*). These internal objective forms, in turn, can induce the functional capacities of the five sense organs upon the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Regarding the identity or difference between these two types of form—the sense organs and their objects—and the consciousness: they are neither identical nor different.

It should be explained according to one's inclination. Therefore, we know that although the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are both termed "form" (*rūpa*), they are distinguished by two meanings:
being with cognition and being without cognition. This is because fundamental ignorance originally possesses two types: first, that which has cognition; second, that which lacks cognition.
If one takes the ignorance of "knowing" as a condition, it can give rise to the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings and the mental factors of the six stages.
If one takes the ignorance of "not knowing" as a condition, it can give rise to phenomena such as mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the receptacle world.
If one takes both types of ignorance—knowing and not knowing—as conditions together, it can then give rise to...

The internal root-body that arises, although consisting of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), nevertheless possesses cognition; thus, the pure material faculties (rūpaprasāda-indriya) are capable of knowing and seeing.

These first five consciousnesses (vijñāna) are designated according to their respective faculties because they possess five characteristics: first, they are consciousnesses that depend upon the faculties.

1. Because consciousness exists in dependence upon the locus of the sense faculty (*indriya*). 2. Because the consciousness produced by two faculties arises only when the faculty is capable of producing it. 3.

Because the consciousness belonging to the faculty follows along with the faculty by means of the seeds of consciousness. 4. Because the consciousness that assists the faculty causes benefit or harm to the faculty depending on whether the consciousness is present or absent.
5. Because the consciousness is like the faculty in being included within the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*).

Because they are subsumed [by these], the first, third, fourth, and fifth [types of compounds] are all *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compounds. Only the second meaning serves as an illustration for the *adhi-bhūmi* (locative) compound;

here, "soil" (*bhūmi*) signifies "son. Although the sense-faculties (*indriya*) receive the name "father" because they can produce consciousness, they are inferior because they merely illuminate the object.
Although consciousness is called the "son," it is superior because it can cognize the object. Since the name is established based on the superior factor, it is called an *adhi-bhūmi* compound.
Commentary on the Verses:
Regarding the nine conditions for the five consciousnesses, the verse states that they arise from seven or eight conditions and have good characteristics that are adjacent.

This explains the meaning of their arising from conditions. As for the "nine conditions," the first is the condition of space (*ākāśa-pratyaya*), which refers to the space between the sense faculty and its object.
1. The condition of the empty space within a crack. 2. The condition of light, namely the three types of luminosity: the sun, the moon, and lamps. 3.

The condition of the sense-faculties (*indriya*), which are the bases upon which the various consciousnesses depend. 4. The condition of the objects (*viṣaya*), which are the objects perceived by the various consciousnesses. 5.

The condition of mental attention (*manasikāra*), which is one of the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). 6. The basis for discrimination, which is the sixth consciousness. 7. Defilement...
The pure support is the seventh consciousness. The eight fundamental supports are the eighth consciousness.
The ninth, the seed-condition, refers to the respective direct seeds of the various consciousnesses. Among these nine conditions, they are subsumed within three of the four conditions.

The seeds within the nine conditions are the first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), among the four conditions. The objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) within the nine is the third, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), among the four.
The remaining seven within the nine are the fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), among the four.

This verse refers to the first five [conditions]; if the latter three are also included, there is another verse that says: "Visual consciousness arises from nine conditions; auditory consciousness only from..."

8. The nose, tongue, and body have seven [objects]; the latter three have five, three, and four [respectively]. If immediate succession (*samanantara*) is added, one is increased from the beginning for each.
Regarding the various consciousnesses arising from conditions: only the eye is fully equipped; the ear hears even in darkness. Excluding light, there are only eight [objects].
The three—nose, tongue, and body—grasp their objects through contact; they can also perceive in the dark. Therefore, excluding space and light, the verse says "the latter three."
That is to say, the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses arise in succession with the fifth, fourth, and third [consciousnesses] as their conditions.

Therefore, the sixth consciousness arises from only five conditions: first, the faculty; second, the object; third, attention (*manasikāra*); fourth, the fundamental [consciousness]; and fifth, the seed.

Beyond the clarity of emptiness, one further eliminates conceptual discrimination because it is the very essence itself; thus, it is not described as defiled or pure, as it is the basis for the sense faculties and their objects.

Furthermore, regarding the seventh consciousness, there are only three conditions: first, the fundamental support (*mūlāśraya*); second, the condition of mental attention (*manasikāra-pratyaya*); and third, the condition of seeds (*bīja-pratyaya*).

It does not mention the sense faculty or the object because the verse states, "It evolves depending on that and takes that as its object," which refers precisely to the fundamental support. Moreover...
Regarding the eighth consciousness arising from four conditions: first, the sense organ; second, the object; third, attention (*manasikāra*); and fourth, the seed.

It does not mention the "root" because that is its very own substance. It does not mention "defilement or purity" because it is the condition of the sense organ. It is "without discrimination" because it does not take the aspect of seeing as its object.
When the verse mentions the "immediately preceding condition," this refers to the second of the four conditions. Each consciousness...

As for its own substance (*svabhāva*): the preceding moment’s cessation serves as the condition to project and produce the subsequent consciousness; because their force and characteristics are identical, it is called "equal" (*samanantara*).

Because there is no intervening obstruction between them, it is called "immediate" (*anantara*). If this condition is added, the eye [consciousness] then possesses ten conditions, and so on up to the eighth.
All [of these] possess five conditions; therefore, it is said that "from the beginning, each increases by one.
Combining the three and separating the two, the verse on observing the sensory world explains the first five consciousnesses.

These consciousnesses perceive objects while carrying their phenomenal marks (*nimitta*), and thus possess the sense of combining and separating. How is this combining and separating known? It is said: consciousness arises from...
Regarding dependent origination: the conditions reveal consciousness. By virtue of the meaning of "depending on conditions," one knows there is the sense of separation and union.

That is to say, among the nine conditions, the two conditions of space and light signify the sense of the separation between the two aspects of the faculties and their objects. Since the visual and auditory consciousnesses both possess the condition of space...
This is cognition through separation (*viprakṛṣṭa-jñāna*). If there were no space as a condition, objects would press against the sense organs;

not only would there be no cognition, but the organs themselves would be damaged. For example, when coarse forms enter the eye, they destroy the eyes; when loud sounds strike the ear, they cause deafness.

Therefore, based on the distinction between damaging and non-damaging the organs, the three [faculties] of nose, tongue, and body do not possess the condition of space; they are cognitions through contact (*saṃnikarṣa-jñāna*).

If the condition of space is present, the sense organs and their objects are separated; because the objects of fragrance, flavor, and touch are not perceived together, [the consciousness] does not know its locus.

If the condition of space is absent, fragrances and odors enter the nose, sourness and saltiness ascend to the tongue, and cold and heat affect the body; as the sense organs and objects conjoin, consciousness perceives and knows them.
Thus, there is a distinction between knowing the locus and not knowing the locus. The verse says "the observer," which refers to the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-portion). It says...
The "dusty world" (saṃsāra) refers to the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), which is termed the five sensory objects (pañcaviṣaya).
For the ignorant, it is difficult to distinguish between consciousness (vijñāna) and the sense faculties (indriya);

thus, the verse speaks of the faculties and consciousness as being easily confused and intermingled, making their distinct meanings difficult to discern. When the verse says "the ignorant," it refers to the Śrāvakas.

A person who exclusively eliminates afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) but does not eliminate cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is therefore called "deluded. What is meant by "difficult to distinguish"? It is said:

because the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their corresponding consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) necessarily share the same object, the five consciousnesses spontaneously encounter their objects and do not give rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

This is the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The five sense organs also operate spontaneously toward their objects; following the force of the causal conditions of the objects, they are likewise non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), and thus said to be difficult to distinguish.

Since they are indeed difficult to distinguish, what is the difference between the sense organs and consciousness? It is said: The five sense organs relate to their objects like a mirror facing a reflection;
although there is an object present, there is for the most part no application of attention (*manasikāra*), nor the arising of desire, intention, or recollection; therefore, they are non-conceptual.

Regarding the five consciousnesses and their objects, they are like images appearing in a mirror. Although they appear as if they were images, there is still attention (*manasikāra*), interest, and the arising of mindfulness;

yet, because they lack the conceptualization of names, words, and categories, they are called "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*). These two points constitute the distinct meanings [of this term]. The old commentary states:
"The Śrāvakas do not know that both the faculties (*indriya*) and the consciousnesses each have seeds and active manifestations (*samudācāra*); they mistake the faculties for the consciousnesses."

They arise mutually. While the seeds and manifestations of the faculties can only induce the seeds and manifestations of consciousness—meaning it is acceptable to say that the faculties serve as the conditions for the arising of consciousness—it is not acceptable to say that they "give rise to" consciousness, because consciousness itself possesses its own seeds capable of producing it. Master Tai said:
"The commentary states that the seeds and manifestations of the faculties and consciousness are distinct; fearing that beginners may still harbor doubts, let me explain further. For..."
The sense organ (*indriya*) is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*), specifically the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is a mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*), specifically the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) of the eighth consciousness. This is the distinction between matter and mind.

Although the sense organ belongs to the category of matter, because it is the direct objective aspect of the eighth consciousness, it alone possesses the two meanings of "appropriation" (*upādāna*) associated with that consciousness. "Appropriation" carries the two senses of "clinging" and "sustaining," as it is the eighth [consciousness]...
It functions to integrate [the objects] into its own essence and to maintain them so they do not disperse. Receptivity (*vedanā*) also possesses two meanings: "receiving" and "experiencing.

It receives [objects] as its domain and causes the arising of experiential awareness. It cannot be compared to external sixfold sense-objects or insentient things; therefore, it shares the same indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) as the eighth consciousness.
As for the mental factors of the five sensory consciousnesses, they possess all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*); thus, the nature of these faculties and consciousnesses differs.
The faculties (*indriya*) can illuminate objects, while consciousness (*vijñāna*) can cognize objects; this is the difference in the functions of the faculties and consciousness.

Generally speaking, both faculties and consciousness are devoid of discrimination (*vikalpa*), and thus they are constantly intermingled. Unless one has refined their analytical understanding, one cannot fully comprehend this; hence it is said that they are "difficult to distinguish. Question:
Since consciousness takes discrimination as its defining characteristic, why do the five sensory consciousnesses lack discrimination? Answer: It is simply...

The absence of conceptual construction (*vitarka*) is called non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*). But does this not mean that there is no subsequent recollective conceptualization (*anusmaranavikalpa*)?
As for the statement that they are "difficult to distinguish," this refers to the Master of the Treatise’s point that the ignorant are unable to distinguish them.

Therefore, for those whose minds are deluded regarding the mental, the Blessed One taught the aggregates (*skandha*); for those deluded regarding form, he taught the bases (*āyatana*); and for those deluded regarding both, he taught the elements (*dhātu*).
Is it not the case that the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are truly difficult to distinguish? If so, what is meant by "difficult to distinguish"? It is said:
from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* down to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, these three categories have been expounded hundreds of thousands of times, yet Ānanda still spoke of "mental cognition" and "ocular vision.
The Buddha then interrogated him with the question: "Can the door see? Judging from this, then—
It can be seen that the distinction between the sense faculties and their consciousnesses is difficult to discern. This concludes the chapter on the contaminated (*sāsrava*).
"Observing emptiness through transformed aspects belongs only to the subsequently attained wisdom; even within the state of fruition, it does not yet directly express the ultimate truth.

This verse refers to the first five types of transformative wisdom (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*). It means that these five cannot directly take *tathatā* (suchness) as their object. As An-hui says: "The first five..."

Since the state of being untainted is already established within the causal stage, one transforms the phenomenal aspect to take True Suchness as its object; for the two aspects—the perceived and the perceiving—are of the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), whereas the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) is of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, the self-verifying aspect directly takes True Suchness as its object.
Because one perceives the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as being without characteristics (*animitta*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"There is an interpretation that the minds and mental factors of the three realms, due to false perfuming (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, although each is a single entity, arise appearing as two—namely, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which are the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).
These two parts exist conventionally but do not exist ultimately; this aspect is called the 'imagined'."

The nature of that which is grasped through conceptual construction is, in reality, dependent upon conditions for its arising; this nature is not non-existent, and is thus called the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because it serves as the basis for that [conceptual] grasping, the Master of the Treatise refutes it with these two lines of verse. "Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) means to manifest or carry along;

"aspect" (*nimitta*) refers to one's own aspect, namely the cognizing mind itself. It means that the cognizing mind manifests and carries along the aspect of its own form, which belongs to the objective essence (*ālambana*).

"Condition" (ālambana) refers to the remote object-condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*). "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) designates the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) which is the subject that perceives. "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) designates the suchness (*tathatā*) which is the object perceived.
Those [masters] maintain that the former five [types of wisdom] involve the perception of signs while taking suchness as their object within the causal stage;

therefore, they are said to "contemplate emptiness. The phrase "only the subsequently attained" excludes the fundamental [wisdom]. Since it is not the fundamental wisdom, it does not directly perceive suchness. "In the fruit" means within the state of Buddhahood. "Expression" (*vyañjana*)...

This is correct. My intention is that the five preceding types of transformative wisdom (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*) do not merely fail to take *tathatā* (suchness) as their object during the stage of causal practice;

even when in the state of the Buddha-fruit, they still lack the sense of directly taking *tathatā* as their object. This is because subsequent wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) necessarily relies on the transformation of the physical sense organs to take objects through their manifested forms.
If fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) were to directly embrace *tathatā* as its substantial object, then in every thought-moment...
That which is associated [with the consciousness] and does not depend on transformed conditions is called the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).

Therefore, among the eight types of consciousness, the first five rely on the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) and possess only subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*); the latter three rely on the mental organ (*manas-indriya*) and thus possess both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom.
"Perfectly luminous, first arising, it becomes untainted; The three types of transformation bodies cease the wheel of suffering.

This verse praises the attainment of the fruit through the five preceding causes. When the mental factors associated with the mind are thus transformed, they become the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
It manifests the three types of transformation bodies to bring to rest the wheel of suffering for sentient beings. "Perfectly luminous" refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

This refers to the stage of Buddhahood. Once the eighth consciousness has been transformed into the pure white consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), the associated mental states immediately become the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Because it manifests suddenly and abruptly, it is said to "first arise. At that time, the first five consciousnesses are likewise able to transform into wisdom.

Therefore, it is said that they "accomplish the untainted" (*anāsrava*). Question: Regarding the first five transformed cognitions (*pariṇāma-jñāna*), why is it said that the eighth [consciousness] is the initial arising of perfect clarity?
Answer: Because the first five faculties are the direct objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness;

since the transforming eighth consciousness is tainted (*sāsrava*), the five faculties it transforms are also tainted. Since the faculties can give rise to consciousness, if the faculties are tainted, the consciousness is also tainted.

Therefore, when the eighth consciousness, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), manifests, the five sense organs and the five consciousnesses all become untainted (*anāsrava*), and the associated mental states likewise transform into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Regarding the three types of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), the *Buddhadhyānasamādhisāgara-sūtra* states that there are three categories of the Buddha’s transformation bodies: first, the Great Transformation Body, which refers to the Tathāgata...

In order to preach the sublime Dharma for the sake of all Bodhisattvas prior to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), causing them to cultivate and advance toward the fruit of Buddhahood, he manifested a great body one thousand *zhang* in height. Second, regarding the minor transformation bodies:

it refers to the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and so forth for the sake of those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings, causing them to abandon delusion and return to the truth, thereby attaining [liberation].
Because he has attained awakening, he manifests a small body of sixteen feet. Third, the manifestation is indeterminate according to the class of beings.
This means that because the Tathāgata’s vows are vast and profound, and his compassion universally covers all, he responds immediately to the resonance of various types of beings;

he may manifest a great body that fills the void of space, or he may manifest a small body, such as one of sixteen or eight feet. Question: Since it is said that consciousness is transformed into wisdom, how is this so?

What is meant by the "associated mental factors" (*cittopakleśa*)? The answer is found in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*: "Although wisdom (*jñāna*) is not consciousness (*vijñāna*), it evolves in dependence upon consciousness;
because consciousness is the primary factor, it is said that consciousness undergoes transformation. Furthermore, in the state of outflows (*sāsrava*), wisdom is weak and consciousness is strong;

in the state without outflows (*anāsrava*), wisdom is strong and consciousness is weak. To encourage sentient beings to rely on wisdom and abandon consciousness, it is therefore said that the eight consciousnesses are transformed."
And one attains these four wisdoms. This concludes the section on the first five consciousnesses.
○ Regarding the sixth consciousness, the verse states that it possesses the three natures, the three means of valid cognition, and pervades the three objects.

The verse [discusses] the sixth consciousness in terms of its nature and magnitude within the context of the subject and object of cognition. "Object" refers exclusively to the cognized (ālambana), while "magnitude" refers exclusively to the cognizer (ālambaka).

Among the three natures (trisvabhāva), both subject and object are pervasive; for when it takes an object such as the wholesome, the cognizing mind itself belongs to that same wholesome nature and so forth.
Because the verse uses the word "pervasive" (tong) to link the preceding and following sections, we know this refers to the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).

The three natures, the three means of valid cognition, and the three objects all apply universally. Regarding the three natures: "wholesome" (kuśala) has the meaning of being concordant and beneficial;

it accords with correct principle and benefits both oneself and others. "Unwholesome" (akuśala) has the meaning of being discordant and harmful; it contradicts correct principle and harms both oneself and others.
Regarding the "unspecified" (*avyākṛta*): it is so called because it is not definitively categorized within the categories of the wholesome or the unwholesome.

Here, the three natures are explained through the meanings of "conducive to benefit" and "contrary to harm. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "That which is conducive to benefit in this world and in future worlds is called 'wholesome' (the nature of goodness;

that which cannot be altered throughout successive lifetimes). Although the fruits of pleasure in the human and celestial realms are conducive to benefit in this world, they are not [conducive to benefit] in..."
Because it pertains to future lives, it is not called "wholesome" (for wholesome fruits follow along with karma, whereas karma is subject to exhaustion).

Because it can cause harm and detriment in both this life and future lives, it is called "unwholesome" (an evil nature that cannot be changed even after changing worlds). Although the bitter fruits of the miserable realms can cause harm in this life, [they do not extend to future lives].
It does not exist in other lifetimes; therefore, it is not an unwholesome result that follows along with karma (because karma is subject to exhaustion).

Since its meaning cannot be definitively categorized as either beneficial or harmful within the context of wholesome or unwholesome states, it is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). The old translation "two time periods" refers precisely to this life and other lifetimes.
This [present] is the current life, while "other" refers to the past and future; thus, it is said that the three natures are also explained in relation to the three time periods.
The three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are as follows: First, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifesting;

it refers to the clear and certain realization of various objects without the accompaniment of verbal designations and without the mind of conjecture, thereby directly apprehending the essence of phenomena. Thus, it is called direct perception. Second, inference (*anumāna*). "Inference" (*anumāna*) means to infer by analogy;

because one knows something exists through the process of inferential estimation, it is so named. For example, seeing smoke from afar, one knows there is fire; or seeing a corner [of an animal] over a wall, one infers its presence.
To know that the other possesses a cow is called inference (*anumāna*). Third, invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*):

this refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) which, when engaging with an object, engage in erroneous discrimination and do not accord with the knowledge of the object; this is called invalid cognition. Question:

Since this is but a single consciousness, how can it be categorized into these three types of valid cognition? Answer: Because the sixth consciousness has five distinct modes: first, the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which engages with...

1. Objects within meditative concentration (*samādhi*): These objects consist of both principles (*tattva*) and phenomena (*dharma*), and they all belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). 2. The independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in the distracted state:

It takes as its object constructed images, matter derived from sensation (*vedanā-nirjāta-rūpa*), and matter consisting of the bases of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) arising from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).

These are generally subsumed under inference (*anumāna*) or are neither [of the two]. 3. The independent mental consciousness in dreams: It takes as its object objects within a dream; these are exclusively invalid cognition (*ayathārtha-jñāna*). 4. Clarity... [text ends]

The sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), shares the same objects as the first five consciousnesses, namely the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). It is common to all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The fifth type of mental consciousness is called "confused mental consciousness" or "distracted mental consciousness. Its objects arise in a state of derangement within the five sense-faculties; for example, like one suffering from a fever who perceives blue as yellow.
