These are all instances of mental consciousness arising through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*); therefore, they are exclusively non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). However...
Regarding the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what constitutes their essential nature? It is said:

non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the primary minds (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) that correctly comprehend while being free from the categories of names and expressions constitute the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Conceptual wisdom (*savikalpa-jñāna*) and the primary minds and mental factors that correctly comprehend by establishing names and expressions constitute the nature of inference (*anumāna*). Erroneous conceptualizations of mind and mental factors constitute invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Regarding the essence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the "three types of objects" are as follows: first, the "objective sphere" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). This refers to actual sense organs and their objects, as well as the "form produced by meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
These arise from their own actual seeds and are the objects of the first five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness.

Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness perceives various real forms without being accompanied by names and phrases, and without a mind of deliberation, this is also called an objective sphere. Moreover, when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) perceives suchness (*tathatā*), it is likewise [an objective sphere].

Regarding these objects, there are two types of "solitary shadow" (duoying) objects. First, the "solitary shadow without a real substrate" (wuzhi duoying), which refers to the objective aspects (xiangfen) transformed by the sixth consciousness when it takes such things as empty flowers, rabbit horns, or the past and future as its objects.
These objective aspects arise from seeds identical to those of the sixth consciousness itself and lack any real substrate such as empty flowers.
Second, the "solitary shadow with a real substrate" (youzhi duoying), which refers to the sixth consciousness taking the seeds and manifestations of the five sense organs as its objects.

Relying upon that as a substrate, a transformed image arises. Because the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) that is thus transformed also arises from the same seed as the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect), there are two types of objects that carry a substrate (*sadravyālambana*):

first, the "true" carrying of a substrate; this occurs when the mind takes the mind as its object, and the intermediate *nimittabhāga* arises from both ends [of the subjective and objective aspects], arising in continuous connection—this is called the true carrying of a substrate.
Second, the "semblance" carrying of a substrate; this occurs when the mind takes [a non-mental object] as its object...

Regarding form (*rūpa*): the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) arises solely from one end of the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part), arising as a transformation that carries [the image]; this is termed "resembling the substantial" (*sad-vastu-sadṛśa*).

The object is the *ālambana* (objective support) and consciousness is the *ālambaka* (subjective perceiver); each possesses its own substance. As for the "real object" (*vastu-gocara*), it takes actual sense organs, sense objects, and the sphere of *tathatā* (suchness) as its substance.
Among those subjective perceivers, with the exception of the *manas* (seventh consciousness), the remaining seven kings and their retinues [are included].

It takes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as its substance. It is a "sole-image" (*kevala-pratibimba*), taking the imagined aspect (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) transformed by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the sixth consciousness as its substance.

Its perceiving subject (*ālambaka*) is precisely the sovereign [consciousness] itself acting as its substance. It is a "substantial-image" (*sadravya-pratibimba*), taking the intermediate imagined aspect transformed [between the object and the subject] as its substance.
Its perceiving subject consists exclusively of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. This is the second verse of this [treatise].

Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) having three types of objects: when the fivefold simultaneous mental consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya-sahaja-manovijñāna*) does not engage in conceptualization, it apprehends the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of its object;

this is the "objective realm" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). When it takes as its object a mind or mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is called the "object with substance" (*sadravya-viṣaya*). When it takes as its object a phenomenon lacking substantial reality (*avastuka-dharma*), it is the "solitary shadow" (*pratibimba-mātra-viṣaya*).

These statements refer to the stage of outflow (*sāsrava*). In the stage of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), the eight consciousnesses can all take the three types of objects as their objects by means of the transformative wisdom (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*).
Because they are based on the provisional and the real, the verse says:

The objective sphere (svabhāva-viṣaya) does not follow the mind; The solitary reflection (pratibimba-mātra) follows only the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga); That which carries a substance (sadravya-sahita) pertains to both the mental object (ālambana) and its intrinsic nature (svabhāva), according to the corresponding seeds and so forth.
The verse explains neutral objects: they arise solely from the seeds of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) and therefore do not follow the mind.

As for what is called "solitary shadow" (*chāyāmātra*), it is a manifestation of one's own mind and thus arises solely from the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect). That which "carries substance" (*sadravya*) arises from both ends; therefore, it pertains to both the mental concomitants (*caitta*) and the fundamental [seeds].
Feeling (*vedanā*) is the mind that takes an object; it is fundamentally the mind that is the object of cognition (*ālambana*), because it takes that which is the object as its essential nature.

Therefore, it has the name "fundamental" (*mūla*). Regarding "nature-seeds" (*prakṛti-bīja*) and so forth: "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the realms (*dhātu*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the three aggregates (*skandha*), and maturation (*vipāka*).

"According to what is appropriate" means that within the categories such as nature-seeds, one should apply them to the three types of objects. Nature (*prakṛti*) refers to the three moral natures. Among these, the "object of nature" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) should not exist [within the category of nature-seeds].

[The seeds] possess the nature of being recorded [in memory]. They may be solitary images (*kevala-pratibimba*) or those that carry a real substrate (*sadravya*). They should be understood as having the nature of being wholesome or unwholesome. "Seed" refers to the causal potential;

it pervades both the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*). Regarding the nature of the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*), within this [classification], it follows the seeds of the object-aspect. Solitary images and those carrying a real substrate follow the seeds of the seeing-aspect. As for their connection to the realms (*dhātu-saṃprayukta*), they pertain to the three realms.
Within this, the objective realm consists only of the five actual sensory objects of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the object-aspect of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The seed-image (bīja-nimitta) and the solitary-image (kevala-nimitta) should pertain to the desire and form realms; they are images of transformation that manifest objects. The image with substance (sadravya-nimitta) should pertain to all three realms, as it is an object transformed in common by both the perceiving mind and the perceived object.

Regarding the three categories, these are the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). Among the five aggregates, the objective realm (svabhāva-viṣaya) should correspond only to the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).

The "sole-image" (duoying) [object] should correspond to the remaining four aggregates (*skandha*). Regarding the "nature-realm" (xingjing) among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it should correspond only to the five internal sense-faculties and the five external objects.
The "sole-image" should correspond only to the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). The "image-with-substance" (dai zhi) should correspond only to the base of the mind-faculty (*manas-āyatana*).

Regarding the "nature-realm" among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), it should correspond only to the ten internal and external elements consisting of faculties and objects. The "sole-image" should correspond only to...

The dharma-object sphere (*dharmadhātu*) and the mental-consciousness sphere (*manovijñānadhātu*) should be understood as being "with-substance" (*sadravya*). Only the seven mental spheres (*cittadhātu*) should be understood as being "maturation" (*vipāka*).

Those that are "objective spheres" (*svabhāvaviṣaya*) are exclusively maturation-form (*vipākārūpa*). Those that are "solely projected images" (*kevalapratibimba*) or "with-substance" are exclusively maturation-mind (*vipākacitta*).

Roughly speaking, objects that are purely material (*rūpa*) consist only of the "nature-aspect" (*svabhāva-ākāra*); those with a shared substance (*sadravya*) consist only of the "mind-aspect" (*citta-ākāra*); and those that are mere images (*pratibimba*) pertain to both.

This is because when the mind takes matter as its object, it transforms and gives rise to an image. Question: Why is it that the sixth consciousness can take all three types of objects? Answer: As stated previously, there are five distinct types of the sixth consciousness.

Excluding the distracted mental consciousness (*vikṣipta-manovijñāna*), the mental consciousness during dreams takes only mere images as its object; the remaining three types all take all three types of objects.

Regarding the object: when the clear and distinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes the five real sensory objects as its common objective support, that which occurs within the state of sudden encounter (*sūtrera-citta*) is termed the "objective realm" (*xingjing*).

If, by means of subsequent moments of thought, one perceives the squareness, roundness, length, or shortness of those five sensory objects, this constitutes a "solitary shadow" (*duying*) based on a real substance.

It is also called "resembling a substantial entity" (*sadṛśa-savastuka*). The solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in its distracted state also operates with respect to three types of objects.
When it first perceives the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), it is an objective reality (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

If it perceives one's own five sense-faculties (*indriya*) or the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of others, it is a "solitary image" (*kevala-pratibimba-viṣaya*), which is also called "resembling a substantial entity. If it perceives one's own present active minds and mental factors...
At that time, this is an object with substance (*sadravya-viṣaya*). The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) also pervades three types of objects:

in the first seven stages (*bhūmi*), during states of contaminated concentration (*sāsrava-samāpatti*), it induces the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) to simultaneously perceive the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); these are thus "objective objects" (*svabhāva-viṣaya*).

Because it can universally perceive dharmas of the three periods of time—whether possessing substance or lacking substance—it is also an "image-only object" (*pratibimba-viṣaya*). Furthermore, when it takes as its object its own mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), it is... [an image-only object].
Regarding the "mixed-reality object":

it is easy to know when the wheel of the three realms turns because the sixth consciousness creates various karmas that cause one to revolve through the three realms; since its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is manifest and predominant, it is said to be "easy."
This can be understood.

Regarding the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*) that are associated with the mind, there are five meanings of "association" (*samprayoga*): first, time, meaning that the primary mind (*citta*) and its factors arise simultaneously; second, basis (*āśraya*), meaning that the primary mind and its factors share the same support...
First, the same basis-faculty (*āśraya-indriya*). Second, the three conditions (*pratyaya*), namely that the king and the subject share the same object of cognition (*ālambana-viṣaya*).

Third, the four modes of activity (*ākāra*), meaning that the modes of the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are identical for both the king and the subject. Fourth, the five entities (*vastu*), namely that the king and the subject each possess the substance of their own self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

Regarding mental factors (*caitta*), there are three meanings: first, they always arise dependent upon the mind; they can only arise by taking the mind as their basis. Second, with... [text truncated]
They are associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*), because contact (*sparśa*) and the others are always associated with the mind.
Three are subordinate to the mind, because contact and the others belong to whichever mind arises at the time they occur.

As for the fifty-one [mental factors], this sixth consciousness is associated with all six categories of mental concomitants (*caitta*). These include the universal (*sarvatraga*), the object-specific (*viniyata*), the wholesome (*kuśala*), and the roots (*mūla*).
Regarding the three delusions (*moha*), among the secondary delusions (*upakleśa*) there are ten major ones common to all. These have been explained in the previous five chapters.

Specifically, the three root-delusions—pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—together with the ten minor secondary delusions and the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*), constitute seventeen dharmas. These will now be explained.
What is pride (*māna*)? Its nature is to be haughty toward others by relying on oneself; its function is to obstruct non-pride and to give rise to suffering.
This means that one who possesses pride does not have a humble mind toward those with virtue or toward virtues themselves;

because of this, they revolve endlessly in the cycle of birth and death and undergo all manner of suffering. What is doubt (*vicikitsā*)? Its nature is hesitation regarding the principles of the Truths (*satya*). It is able to...
Its function is to obstruct the absence of doubt regarding wholesome qualities; that is to say, because wholesome states do not arise in one who is hesitant. What is wrong view?
It has the nature of defiled wisdom that seeks after the principles of the truths in a distorted manner. Its function is to obstruct right view and to bring about suffering;

that is to say, because one who holds wrong views undergoes much suffering. Although this view is the same in its general mode of activity, it is differentiated into five types. Though they are alike...
Its nature is defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭa-prajñā*). Because its functional activities differ, it is divided into five types: 1. **The view of a self-identity** (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*):

This refers to the grasping at "I" and "mine" with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*). Its function is to serve as the basis for all speculative views. 2. **The view of extremes** (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*):

This refers to the adherence to either annihilationism or eternalism with respect to those same aggregates. Its function is to obstruct the departure [from suffering] via the Middle Way. 3. **False view** (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*)... [text continues]
The view [of nihilism] has as its function the denial of cause, effect, activity, and substantial reality.

The adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists in grasping at various views and their underlying aggregates as being supreme and capable of bringing about purification; its function is to serve as the basis for all conflict and strife.

The fifth is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This refers to the grasping at those precepts and observances that accord with various views, as well as the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which they depend, as being supreme and capable of bringing about purification.
Its function is to serve as a basis for fruitless exertion and suffering. This concludes the explanation of the three fundamental [afflictions].

The following explains the ten minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*). What is anger (*krodha*)? Its nature is the outburst of indignation based upon a presently manifest object that is disadvantageous.
Its function is to obstruct non-anger and to result in the grasping of weapons. That is to say, one who harbors anger frequently manifests violent and evil behavior.

Because it is a bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*), its essence consists of a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*). This is because there is no separate characteristic or function of anger (*krodha*) apart from hatred.
What is resentment (*upanāha*)? Having anger as its precursor, it is the nature of harboring malice without relinquishing it and binding oneself in enmity.

Its function is to obstruct the absence of resentment and to cause feverish affliction (*paridāha*). That is to say, one who harbors resentment cannot endure [the offense] and is constantly tormented by heat. This...
It also has a portion of *pratigha* (hostility) as its essence, because there is no distinct characteristic or function of *upanāha* (resentment) apart from hostility. What is *mrakṣa* (concealment)?
Its nature is to hide one's own committed transgressions out of fear of losing profit and reputation. Its function is to obstruct the absence of concealment and to cause remorse and distress;

that is to say, one who conceals a transgression will inevitably experience remorse and distress later on, due to a lack of peace and stability. This consists of two parts: greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*).

It has [resentment] as its essence. What is vexation (*pradāsa*)? Having resentment and hatred as its precursor, it is characterized by a violent heat that pursues and contacts [the object]; its nature is ferocity;
its function is to obstruct non-vexation and to act as stinging irritation. This means that when one pursues past evils and encounters present adverse conditions, the mind becomes ferocious.
It frequently gives rise to clamorous and violent, wicked, and coarse speech for the purpose of stinging others like maggots;

this too has a portion of *pratigha* (hatred) as its essence, because there is no distinct characteristic or function of *upāyāsa* (malice) apart from hatred. What is *īrṣyā* (envy)? Its nature is jealousy, characterized by a preoccupation with one’s own fame and profit and an inability to endure the prosperity of others.
Its function is to obstruct non-envy and to produce grief and distress. That is to say, one who is envious, upon hearing—
Seeing the prosperity of others, one harbors deep sorrow and distress because of a lack of inner peace;
this too has a portion of *dveṣa* (hatred) as its essence, for apart from hatred, there is no separate characteristic or function of envy (*īrṣyā*). What is stinginess (*mātsarya*)?

Its nature is to be secretive and parsimonious regarding wealth and the Dharma, being unable to give or relinquish them. Its activity is to cause base accumulation, which serves to obstruct non-stinginess. That is to say, the mind of one who is stingy is largely...
It is base and coarse. Because one is unable to relinquish the accumulation of wealth and property, this has as its essence a portion of craving (*lobha*).

Since there is no distinct characteristic or function of stinginess apart from craving, it is so designated. What is deception? It is the feigning of possessing virtuous qualities for the sake of gaining profit and reputation.
Deceit (*māyā*) has guile as its intrinsic nature; it functions to obstruct non-deception and has wrong livelihood as its activity.

This refers to those who are hypocritical and deceptive, harboring ulterior motives and frequently manifesting what is unreal due to their pursuit of wrong livelihood. Its essence consists of a portion of greed and delusion, for apart from these two, there is no distinct characteristic or function of deception.
What is flattery (*śāṭhya*)? It is the fabrication of artificial deportment for the purpose of deceiving others; it is crookedness.
It has the nature of flattery (*śāṭhya*) and functions to obstruct honest instruction.

That is to say, one who is flatteringly crooked seeks to deceive others by bending to suit the occasion and contriving expedients to win over their favor, or by concealing one's own faults, thereby failing to submit to the correct instruction of teachers and friends.
This also takes a portion of greed and delusion as its essence; apart from these two, there is no separate characteristic or function of flattery.
Therefore, what is harm (*vihiṃsā*)? It has as its nature the lack of compassion toward sentient beings and the intent to injure and afflict them;
it functions as an obstacle to non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) and has the activity of causing distress and oppression. This is because one who harms others causes them distress and oppression.

Furthermore, this has a portion of hatred (*vyāpāda*) as its essence, for apart from hatred, there is no distinct characteristic or function of harm. The specific characteristics of hatred and harm should be understood by analogy with their wholesome counterparts.
What is *mada* (arrogance)? It is the nature of being intoxicated and haughty due to deep attachment to one's own prosperity;
its function is to obstruct non-arrogance and to serve as a basis for defilement. This is because one who is intoxicated by *mada* gives rise to all manner of defiled phenomena.

Furthermore, this has a portion of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its essence, for apart from craving, there is no separate characteristic or function of *mada*. The explanation of the minor derivative afflictions is now complete.

The following explains the indeterminate factors (*aniyata*). The treatise states: Regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra are called "indeterminate" because they are not fixed as being either wholesome, defiled, or otherwise;

unlike contact (*sparśa*) and so forth, which necessarily pervade the mind, nor like desire (*chanda*) and so forth, which necessarily pervade the ground [of all minds]. Thus, they are designated by the name "indeterminate."
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) refers to *akukṛta*. Its nature is the subsequent regret for actions performed poorly; its function is to obstruct meditative stillness (*śamatha*).
This is a case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect, because one first performs an action poorly and only subsequently feels regret.
Regret for not having previously performed an action is also subsumed under *akukṛta*, as in the expression of regret: "I previously did not perform such a task; this is my fault."
"Sleep" (*middha*) refers to drowsiness; its nature is to cause the body to lose its mastery and to be characterized by obscurity and brevity. Its function is to obstruct insight (*vipaśyanā*).

This means that in the state of sleep, the body lacks mastery and the mind is extremely dark and feeble because it functions through a single sense-door. The term "obscurity" serves to distinguish it from [the mental state] occurring during meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Briefly distinguishing the state of wakefulness serves to demonstrate that sleep possesses both essence and function; it is not devoid of them. *Vitarka* (applied thought) refers to seeking;
its nature is coarse mental activity directed toward the objects of mental discourse, causing the mind to be hurried. *Vicāra* (sustained thought) refers to examination;

its nature is subtle mental activity directed toward the objects of mental discourse, causing the mind to be hurried. Both of these [operate] upon the states of the body and mind, whether they are settled or unsettled.
Its function is to serve as a basis. Both take a portion of *vitarka* (investigation) and *vicāra* (analysis) based on wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence.

This is because there is a distinction between the categories of meaning: those that do not involve deep deliberation and those that do involve deep deliberation regarding the objects of mental discourse (*manojalpa*). For if one were to exclude wisdom, the distinct essential natures of these two—*vitarka* and *vicāra*—could not be established.
What is meant by "objects of mental discourse"? It refers to objects apprehended by the mind that for the most part rely upon names and expressions.
Therefore, they are called the objects of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*). Regarding remorse, torpor, vitarka, and vicāra: which are provisional and which are real?

It is said: Remorse and torpor are real; vitarka and vicāra are provisional. Why are they considered provisional? It is said: Both take a portion of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence.
If they cause the mind to be at ease, they belong to the category of volition; if they cause the mind to be uneasy, they belong to the category of wisdom. Why is this so? Volition is... [gradual]...
Because [the mind] is subtle, wisdom is urgent and coarse. If this is the case, when one seeks to settle the mind, one employs volition (*cetanā*) without wisdom;
when it is not settled, one employs wisdom without volition. How can you say they are used together? The Master Tongzhao explained that there is both the auxiliary and the primary.
If volition is used as the primary, the urgent wisdom follows volition and is able to settle the mind. If wisdom is used as the primary, slowly...
Volition follows wisdom and causes the mind to be unsettled. If explained in this way, there is no contradiction in their simultaneous operation;
they are to be applied separately according to the circumstances of good or evil.

Regarding the sixth consciousness, it functions together with fifty-one mental factors (caitta), following conditions and pursuing objects; when encountering the wholesome, it becomes a wholesome mind.
They correspond with what they encounter: when encountering the unwholesome, the unwholesome mind corresponds with it.
The heterodox and the orthodox are thus clearly distinguished and do not become confused; hence it is said that they are "individually assigned."
"Nature, realm, and feeling—these three constantly transform; the faculties and mental factors, such as faith and so forth, are all interconnected.
(Verse 6) The sixth consciousness constantly undergoes transformation and change within the three categories of nature (*svabhāva*), realm (*dhātu*), and feeling (*vedanā*);

thus, the various mental factors (*caitta*) follow it, which is why they are said to be "interconnected. "Nature" refers to the three natures, such as the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth. "Realm" refers to the [three] realms, such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.

The three realms. "Feeling" refers to the three types of feeling, namely suffering and so forth. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "These six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and unstable;
therefore, they are all capable of being associated with the three feelings. This is because they all experience objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neither.

Experiencing the aspect of an agreeable object, which brings gratification to body and mind, is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*). Experiencing the aspect of a disagreeable object, which oppresses body and mind, is called..."

That which is called the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) is that which experiences an object of moderate intensity; it is neither oppressive nor pleasant for either body or mind, and is thus called the sensation of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhā-vedanā*).
Alternatively, they are called the five sensations, because suffering is divided into sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and pleasure is divided into joy (*saumanasya*). Therefore, the treatise further states:

"Among the three [sensations], suffering and pleasure are each divided into two" because the characteristics of that which oppresses and that which pleases the body and mind are distinct. This is due to the absence of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpanāt*).

Because there is conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), there is a distinction between what is heavy and what is light. Because there is differentiation, that which is neither painful nor pleasant is not divided into two, as it is neither oppressive nor gratifying;
this is because its characteristics are non-distinct, it is free from conceptual differentiation, and it functions with equanimity.

These five sensations (*vedanā*) exist either partially or in their entirety within the eight consciousnesses. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses possess only the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). They are [therein] indeterminate.

The [mental] faculty operates upon its object. There are no other four feelings (vedanā). The first five *pravṛtti-vijñānas* are associated only with the three feelings of suffering (*duḥkha*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "These three feelings are each further divided into two. Those associated with the five consciousnesses are called bodily feelings (*kāyikī vedanā*);

those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are called mental feelings (*caitasikī vedanā*). Since the meaning of these three feelings was omitted in the preceding five chapters, they are presented here.

This is clarified as follows. Regarding the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the two masters differ in their explanations: one asserts that it is devoid of suffering and is associated only with four feelings (*vedanā*);

the other asserts that it possesses suffering, because it is associated with all five feelings. This is discussed in detail within the treatise, which establishes that the sixth consciousness must necessarily be associated with all five feelings.
The term "root" (*mūla*) in the verse refers to the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). "Secondary" (*anu*) refers to the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

"Faith" (*śraddhā*) is one among the eleven factors within the category of wholesome mental states. The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes the remaining ten factors, as well as those that are universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viniyata*), and indeterminate (*aniyata*).

These various mental factors—both defiled and pure—are associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and constantly evolve throughout the three [realms of] existence, the various destinies, and the three types of feeling (*vedanā*).
It is easy [to understand].

When the body moves and speech is uttered, it is the sixth consciousness alone that is the primary agent of praise, for its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is most excellent because it possesses three kinds of volition (*cetanā*). The first is the volition of deliberation (*nirūpaṇa-cetanā*), which means:

1. The volition of deliberation (*tulanā-cetanā*): because there is no active construction at this stage. 2. The volition of determination (*niścaya-cetanā*): because once the mind has reached a decision, there is something to be performed.
3. The volition of initiation (*abhisamskāra-cetanā*): "initiation" refers to initiating the body and initiating speech. The volition that initiates the body is called bodily action (*kāyakarma*);
the volition that initiates speech is called vocal action (*vākkarma*). Since volition itself is action, the volition of initiation constitutes bodily [action].
Vocal action consists of the first two types of volition (*cetanā*), as these are mental actions (*manas-karman*).

The power of karma that projects (*ākṣepa*) and completes (*paripūraṇa*)—which draws forth the three aforementioned types of action—is capable of producing both the projected and the completed results. That which produces the eighth [moment] is called the "projecting" of the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*).

That which acts as the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) is able to summon the first six [consciousnesses]; that which brings about the full ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) is called completing karma (*paripūrakakarman*). Regarding what is termed "projecting":
if it is associated with the eleven factors of the wholesome state, one is projected by wholesome karma into the realms of humans and devas;

if it is associated with the afflictions of the root and secondary [defilements], one is projected by unwholesome karma into the three miserable destinies. Or, it refers to the conduct of a single lifetime.
Evil. At the time of death, if a wholesome mind is intensely powerful, one will be drawn by that forceful karma to be born in a good realm.
Conversely, even if one has practiced virtue in this life, if the evil karma of previous lives has ripened, one will be drawn by that matured karma to be born in an evil realm.
Just as a shadow follows a form, it is called "drawing" (*ākṣepa*). Because the power of karma is predominant and capable of drawing one along, it is termed "projecting karma" (*ākṣepaka-karma*).

Because it completes the total fruit, it is called "fulfilling karma" (*pūrṇakarma*). It is like a master painter and his apprentice: one creates the outline and the other fills in the colors. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"One karma draws forth one fruit; many karmas can fulfill it. Furthermore, there are four permutations:

(1) one karma drawing forth one fruit; (2) one karma drawing forth many fruits; (3) many karmas drawing forth one fruit; and (4) many karmas drawing forth many fruits. All of these are based on the initial [projecting cause].

The projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) serves as the inducement, while the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*) serves as the fulfillment. Now, the volition (*cetanā*) that constitutes the projecting karma must necessarily arise from the sixth mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).

As for the volition that constitutes the completing karma, it may arise from the five sensory consciousnesses; however, since the five [sensory] consciousnesses lack conceptual grasping (*nirvikalpa*), they cannot independently create karma.
Even when completing karma is produced, it is not through their own power, but only by being induced by the mental consciousness that they are able to do so.

This is because [the first five consciousnesses] possess both wholesome and unwholesome natures. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses cannot perform such creation, as they are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).
However, when discussing which of the eight consciousnesses invites karma and brings about its fruition, it is only the eighth that does so, precisely because it is of an indeterminate nature.

The first six [consciousnesses] are also partially [unobscured-indeterminate], because they are also indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If it is not produced by karma, it belongs exclusively to the seventh [consciousness], because its nature is obscured (*nivṛta*).
The first six are also partially [obscured-indeterminate], because their nature is both wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*). This concludes the section on the tainted (*sāsrava*).
"Having initiated the first mind on the Stage of Joy, the innate [afflictions] still manifest as latent tendencies.

This verse refers to the sixth consciousness and the meaning of the transformation of inferior-grade wisdom. Regarding the grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), there are two types each:

first, the innate (*sahaja*); second, the discriminative (*vikalpita*). The innate grasping at self and phenomena has proceeded from beginningless time through the internal perfuming of false conceptualizations.
Due to the power of its cause, it is always coexistent with the body; it does not depend on false teachings or false discrimination, but functions spontaneously.

Therefore, it is called "innate" (*sahaja*). This, moreover, is of two kinds: first, that which is constantly continuous, residing in the seventh consciousness, taking the eighth consciousness as its object, giving rise to the appearances of its own mind, and grasping at them as real self and phenomena; second, that which is intermittent, residing in the sixth consciousness, taking consciousness as its object.

Regarding the objects of cognition—the characteristics of the aggregates, bases, and elements—whether taken collectively or individually—one gives rise to mental images and clings to them as a real self and real dharmas.

These two [clinging to self and dharmas] arise together; because they are subtle, they are difficult to sever. Throughout the subsequent ten stages, one repeatedly cultivates the superior contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness.
Only then can it be eliminated. The conceptualization of self and phenomena also arises due to the power of external conditions in the present;
it does not coexist with the body. It must wait for false teachings and false discrimination before it subsequently arises, and is therefore called "conceptual" (*vikalpa*).
It exists solely within the sixth consciousness. This also has two types: first, that which takes as its object the aggregates, bases, and elements as taught in false teachings.
Regarding the first: based on the characteristics of the signs of one’s own mind, one engages in conceptualization and deliberation, grasping at them as a real self and real dharmas.

Regarding the second: based on the characteristics of the *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) and so forth as taught by false teachings, one engages in conceptualization and deliberation, grasping at them as a real self and real dharmas.

These two types of self and dharmas are coarse and thus easy to sever; upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one contemplates the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the twofold emptiness of all dharmas, and is thereby able to...
It is eliminated. The verse speaks of "joy," which refers to the first stage (*bhūmi*). What is meant by "arising"? It is said: because it is the initial transformation of wisdom.

Through the sixth consciousness, there is a threefold transformation of wisdom: at the first stage, it transforms in its inferior grade; at the eighth stage, it transforms in its middling grade; and at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it transforms in its superior grade.
Because the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) eliminates only the dualistic grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), it is designated as the inferior grade.

[Question: What is called the "initial mind"? [Answer: It is said that within a single stage (*bhūmi*), there are three kinds of mind: namely, entering, abiding, and emerging. The very first moment of entering a stage is what is termed the "initial mind.
"Enveloping" (*paryavasthāna*) refers to active manifestation (*samudācāra*); "slumbering" (*anuśaya*) refers to the seeds (*bīja*). This is because at the time of ascending to the stages...
Because the innate seeds and manifestations have not yet been completely subdued and extinguished, it is said that they still "manifest as active entanglements and latent tendencies.

After the Stage of Far-Going (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi), there is exclusively the untainted (*anāsrava*). The verse "Observing with perfect clarity, illuminating the great trichiliocosm" refers to the sixth consciousness.
It concerns the meaning of the transformation of wisdom (*jñāna-parāvṛtti*) at the medium and superior levels. The Stage of Far-Going is the seventh stage. "After" [refers to] the subsequent stages.

The term "character" (*akṣara*) refers to the final three stages up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). This means that upon entering the eighth stage, although the transformation of wisdom is of medium grade, it is not yet ultimate;

only upon reaching Equal Enlightenment does the transformation become of the highest grade, and thus it is called "perfectly luminous. Question: Regarding the severance of the delusions of conceptual discrimination:

When one first realizes the two kinds of emptiness, it is naturally of an inferior grade (*mṛdu*). To sever the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), one ought to do so only at the superior grade (*adhimātra*);

how then could there be a middle grade? It is said: Because the innate grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) are distinct obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), when ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*), although the innate grasping at a self is said to be suddenly suppressed (*vibhava*), the innate grasping at phenomena is gradually suppressed and gradually severed throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), until it becomes purely untainted (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, since the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) also occasionally involve outflows (*sāsrava*), when Bodhisattvas in the first seven stages intentionally give rise to the affliction of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) while delivering sentient beings, this is termed "with effort" (*sābhoga*).
Upon reaching the eighth stage, as the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is relinquished, self-grasping is forever suppressed;
this is termed "without effort" (*anābhoga*). Although grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persists, it is transformed such that only the medium grade remains. Only...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The category of mind associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), specifically the category of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), may first arise during the stage of vision (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles.

Thereafter, it proceeds successively until the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), or until the end of the Bodhisattva stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) (which is the inferior transformation);

or it reaches the higher stages, provided they are not contaminated (*sāsrava*) (which is the middling transformation); or it may occur at times when there is no mental activity; in all these cases, it is permissible."

The category of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) first arises during the Bodhisattva’s stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*). This constitutes the "inferior transformation" (*mṛdu-parāvṛtti*).

Thereafter, as one progresses through the successive stages up to the highest level, whenever it is not a contaminated state—namely, during the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), or at times when there is no mind—it is possible for this to manifest.
(This concludes the explanation of the "transformation within the cause," hence the phrase "it is possible"). What, then, is called the "superior transformation" (*adhimātra-parāvṛtti*)?

Yes. It is said: In the stage of ultimate fruition (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted, and they no longer increase in accordance with [the mind]. Its nature is pure and perfectly luminous;
this is called the superior transformation. The chapter on the sixth consciousness is concluded.
Verse on the Seventh Consciousness:

It possesses a "quality-borne" object (*saviṣaya*), is obscured (*nivṛta*), and pervades both the sentient and the fundamental. Following conditions, it clings to a self; its mode of cognition is non-valid (*abhūta*).
This verse concerns the seventh consciousness. Among the three types of objects, it takes only the "quality-borne" object (*saviṣaya*). Among the four natures, it is "obscured" (*nivṛta*).
Commentary: Among the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this is merely non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Regarding what is called "an object with a core" (*sanimitta-viṣaya*):

because the mind takes the mind as its object, the intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) arises from both ends and arises in connection with them. This explains the "object with a core" as that which pervades both the phenomenal (*nirmāṇa*) and the fundamental (*mūla*).
The seventh consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) is the cognizing mind; because it constantly gives rise to grasping, it is termed "phenomenal" (*nirmāṇa*). The eighth...
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is the "essence" (*mūla*), because it serves as the objective essence (*ālambana-vastu*).

The intermediate image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is called "pervasive" (*sāmānya*), because it arises from both ends [of the seeing-part and the essence]. The mind that acts as the perceiver manifests the image-part, which resembles the objective essence.
It is called "possessing substance" (*sābhāsā*). This [manas] is associated with the four afflictions and so forth;

because these are defiled dharmas, they obstruct the Noble Path and conceal the true mind, and are therefore termed "obscured" (*nivṛta*). Because they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).

What is the name and what is the meaning? It is named "affliction" (*kleśa*). To explain: the first is self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), which refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) that is deluded regarding the characteristic of a self.
First, delusion regarding selflessness; second, the view of a self, which refers to the grasping at a self because one falsely clings to a self within phenomena that are not-self;
third, self-conceit, which refers to arrogance because the mind becomes uplifted by relying on the grasped self;
and fourth, self-love, which refers to craving for a self because of deep attachment to the grasped self. Because these four afflictions are present, [they] follow...

Taking the eighth consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) as its object, it clings to it as "self. Since the eighth consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* serves as the objective essence (*ālambana-svabhāva*), it is fundamentally not the self;
yet it falsely clings to it as the self, failing to accord with that essence. The intermediate *nimitta-bhāga* (image part) arises through transformation at both ends;
it is fundamentally not the self, yet it falsely clings to it as the self, failing to accord with the image part. Because it does not accord with either of these two objects, it is so named.

[This is] not a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The eight universal [mental factors], the five object-specific ones, wisdom (*mati*), greed, delusion, self-view, and pride accompany the seventh consciousness; these are the mental factors associated with it. There are only the eight great universal [factors] and the five universal [factors]. Among the five object-specific ones: *Note:

This is a partial translation of the verse and commentary regarding the mental factors associated with the seventh *manas-vijñāna*. The full list of the eight great universal factors (mahābhūmika) includes: sensation, conceptualization, volition, contact, attention, desire, resolve, and mindfulness. The five universal factors (sarvatraga) are: initial mental application, sustained mental application, discernment, determination, and mindfulness. The five object-specific factors (viśeṣabhūmika) are: desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.*

...and wisdom (*prajñā*). Among the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), greed (*lobha*), delusion (*moha*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*)—these together constitute eighteen [mental factors]. Question: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "There is an interpretation that these mental factors associated with the *manas* are only nine: the first four and the latter five, which together make nine. How can this be consistent with [the claim that they] coexist with the eight [root afflictions] and wisdom? Answer: If *styāna* (sloth) were absent, there would necessarily be no lack of functional capacity (*akarmanyatā*). Therefore, [the presence of] *styāna* is required. Furthermore, since the *manas* is always accompanied by the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it must also be accompanied by the other [afflictions] such as greed, for they are mutually dependent. Thus, it is established that the *manas* is always associated with these ten mental factors. As for the statement that there are only nine, this refers to the fact that the view of self-existence and the conceit of self-existence (*asmimāna*) are subsumed within the category of "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). Consequently, when one speaks of the "eight great [afflictions]," the view of self-existence and the conceit of self-existence are included therein. Wisdom is not mentioned because it does not arise from the power of ignorance; rather, it arises from the power of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Since the *manas* is always defiled, it is not associated with wisdom. However, because the view of self-existence and the conceit of self-existence are both forms of view, they are subsumed under the single heading of "view," and thus the number of mental factors is said to be nine. This is the meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. In the *Triṃśikā*, however, it is stated: "The view of self-existence and the conceit of self-existence are always present. This indicates that although these two are distinct entities, they are subsumed under the single category of "view" due to their commonality. Therefore, the *Triṃśikā* speaks of ten mental factors, while the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* speaks of nine. There is no contradiction between the two. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The view of self-existence and the conceit of self-existence are always present. What treatise states that these three mental factors are associated with defiled minds? Therefore, a defiled mind is necessarily produced in association with all eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Since wisdom (*prajñā*) has the nature of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is also appropriate for it to be present [among them].

Question: Among the six root afflictions, the views are expanded to form ten; why is there only this fourfold [classification] here? Answer: Because the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is included [within it].
Other views do not arise. Because this view is characterized by decisive certainty, doubt has no room to arise. Furthermore, because there is attachment to a self, hatred cannot arise.
Therefore, the afflictions associated with this consciousness are only four. For what reason does this consciousness lack other mental factors, such as desire?

Hope is the seeking of what has not yet been attained; this consciousness functions spontaneously, taking as its object what is already attained and thus has nothing to hope for, and therefore it possesses no desire (*chanda*).

Admiration (*adhimokṣa*) is the mental impression and maintenance of an object that has never before been determined; this consciousness, being beginningless, constantly takes a determined object as its focus.
Because it is not sustained by the *sūtras*, there is no resolve (*adhimokṣa*). Mindfulness (*smṛti*) merely recollects things previously experienced;

since this consciousness always takes as its object a presently perceived realm and does not involve recollection, it lacks mindfulness. Concentration (*samādhi*) consists solely in binding the mind to focus one-pointedly on a single object;
since this consciousness functions spontaneously, taking different objects moment by moment, it is not one-pointed and thus lacks concentration. It is virtuous (*kuśala*).

Because it is pure, this consciousness does not coexist with them. Furthermore, the ten [afflictions] such as anger have coarse and agitated modes of activity (*ākāra*), whereas this consciousness is subtle and refined; therefore, it does not coexist with them.

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), whereas this [consciousness] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); thus, it does not share their characteristics.

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) involves regretting actions previously committed, whereas this consciousness functions spontaneously and constantly takes present objects as its domain; it is not characterized by regret.

Because it is the result of prior karma, there is no sense of regret (*kaukṛtya*). Sleep necessarily depends on the heaviness and dullness of body and mind, and arises only temporarily through the power of external conditions.
This consciousness, however, is a single-classed internal grasping from beginningless time that does not depend on external conditions; therefore, those [states] do not exist for it.
Vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) both operate by way of the external door; they involve shallow or deep deliberation and the utterance of coarse or subtle speech.
This consciousness, however, operates solely by way of the internal door, as it is of a single type that clings to a self; therefore, it does not coexist with them.

(Verse on the Seventh Consciousness) Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and mode of activity (*ākāra*) both consist of deliberation (*manana*). Therefore, it constantly follows the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness, grasping it as a self.

Regarding its mode of activity (*ākāra*): since the mental faculty (*manas*) has reflection as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it likewise employs that very [reflection] as its mode of activity.

By this, the specific name established for it is also explained: because it is able to reflectively deliberate, it is called *manas*. This refers to the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Because one constantly and thoroughly deliberates upon the characteristics of the grasped self, and because even in the stage of having already transformed the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one also thoroughly deliberates upon the characteristic of non-self, "constant" and "thorough" are analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) among the eight consciousnesses: 1. Constant but not thorough:
This refers to the eighth consciousness. It does not grasp a self, yet it is uninterrupted. 2. Thorough but not constant: This refers to the sixth [consciousness].

Therefore, Dharmapāla said: "In the fifth and eighth [consciousnesses], there is neither dharma nor person; in the sixth and seventh, there is..."
The consciousnesses are all equally balanced. The five and the eighth are without grasping; the sixth and the seventh possess grasping—this is the meaning of "equally balanced.

Among the five, the eighth, and the first, one is eternal and one is non-eternal; likewise, among the sixth and the seventh, one is eternal and one is non-eternal—this too is the meaning of "equally balanced.

That sentient beings are perpetually deluded day and night—"perpetually" (zhèn) means "constantly" (ān)—refers to the seventh consciousness, because it constantly grasps at a self, thereby causing [sentient beings] to exist...
Sentient beings constantly dwell in the long night, at ease in their delusion and unaware of it themselves.
The four afflictions and eight major [afflictions] arise in conjunction; the six evolving consciousnesses are called the basis for defilement and purity.
This refers back to the consciousness associated with the aforementioned defilements, which causes sentient beings to remain in delusion day and night, obstructing the true meaning.
